qs.q: The decrease in cell size seen in atrophy is primarily mediated by which of the following?
o: Increased protein synthesis and cellular expansion
Decreased protein degradation and slower turnover
Increased autophagy and enhanced proteasome activity
qs.e: Atrophy involves increased degradation of cellular components through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and autophagy, leading to decreased cell size. Increased protein synthesis would lead to hypertrophy instead.
qs.s: Cell Injury & Adaptation — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A child residing in a developing country exhibits growth stunting and small intestinal histological changes that closely resemble severe coeliac disease, including villous atrophy, but without accepted diagnostic criteria or proven treatment. What condition is this?
qs.e: Environmental enteropathy affects millions of children in developing countries, histologically resembling coeliac disease with villous atrophy, but lacks proven treatment or standard diagnostic criteria. Irritable bowel syndrome shows no structural or microscopic abnormalities.

qs.q: A peripheral blood smear from an asplenic adult patient with sickle cell anemia is reviewed in the laboratory. Which of the following classic morphological findings is most likely to be seen due to functional splenic atrophy?
qs.e: Features of splenic atrophy, such as Howell-Jolly bodies, are characteristically found on peripheral blood smears due to autosplenectomy by adolescence or early childhood. Heinz bodies are seen in G6PD deficiency.

qs.q: An infant presents with intractable watery diarrhea in the first week of life that continues even when the patient is kept NPO (nil per os). Intestinal biopsy shows villus atrophy and intracytoplasmic inclusions lined by intact microvilli. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Microvillous atrophy-inclusion disease is characterized by watery diarrhea that persists despite NPO status and diagnostic intracytoplasmic inclusions on biopsy. Other congenital enteropathies typically improve with cessation of oral intake or show tufting features.

qs.q: A neonate develops early-onset severe intractable watery diarrhea within the first days of life with impaired growth. Intestinal biopsy shows villus atrophy with focal crowding and disorganization of surface enterocytes forming crypt pseudocysts resembling tufts. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Intestinal epithelial dysplasia (tufting enteropathy) is characterized by focal enterocyte crowding resembling tufts and dilated crypts with pseudocysts. Microvillous atrophy features intracytoplasmic inclusions rather than epithelial tufts.

qs.q: A 32-year-old male develops painful testicular swelling following a viral infection. Histological examination shows a prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with patchy tubular atrophy. What is the most likely etiology?
qs.e: Mumps orchitis typically complicates mumps infection in adult males and features a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate that can lead to fibrosis and sterility. Bacterial orchitis usually shows a neutrophilic rather than a lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory pattern.
qs.s: Male Reproductive Pathology: Comprehensive Review — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which gastrointestinal motility complication is most directly linked to smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis in the lower esophagus?
o: Outlet obstruction of the gastric pylorus
Bacterial overgrowth in the large bowel
qs.e: Smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis in the lower esophagus lead to reduced sphincter tone and acid reflux with erosive esophagitis. Small intestine and large bowel involvement typically lead to malabsorption and pseudo-obstruction rather than lower esophageal reflux.

qs.q: A study documents testicular abnormalities in adult males with infertility, some having a patchy pattern of atrophy of testicular tubules. Which of the following infections is most likely to produce these findings?
qs.e: This is a very common childhood infection (when vaccinations are not done) resulting in orchitis as well as parotitis. The inflammation rarely causes enough damage to produce a significantly reduced sperm count if acquired in childhood. The virus tends to produce more testicular damage when adults are infected.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Atrophy is a decrease in the size of a cell, tissue, or organ. It results from reduced workload, denervation, loss of hormonal stimulation, inadequate nutrition, or aging. Microscopically, it involves shrinkage of cells and often an increase in apoptosis.

sections.p: Atrophy is the irreversible decrease in the size of an organ or tissue due to cell shrinkage. Diagnosis is typically made by clinical examination and confirmed with imaging or biopsy, depending on the affected organ.
b: Characterised by reduced cell size and number.
Can affect any organ or tissue.

t.b: To assess organ size and detect structural changes suggestive of atrophy.
To examine tissue microscopically for cellular shrinkage and loss.

sections.p: Severity is usually described qualitatively as mild, moderate, or severe based on the degree of tissue loss and functional impairment. There are no formal staging systems for general atrophy.
b: Mild atrophy: minimal functional deficit.
Moderate atrophy: noticeable functional impairment.
Severe atrophy: significant loss of function, potentially life-threatening.

sections.p: Causes vary by organ but include disuse, denervation, lack of trophic signals (hormonal or growth factors), inadequate nutrition, and aging. Ischemia can also lead to atrophy.
b: Disuse atrophy (e.g., limb in cast).
Denervation atrophy (e.g., nerve injury).
Hormonal atrophy (e.g., hypopituitarism).
Nutritional deficiency (e.g., severe malnutrition).
Aging (senile atrophy).

sections.p: Presentation depends on the affected organ. It can range from asymptomatic to significant functional decline. For example, muscle atrophy causes weakness, while brain atrophy may lead to cognitive decline.
b: Muscle weakness and reduced bulk.
Cognitive impairment or neurological deficits.
Reduced organ-specific function (e.g., endocrine insufficiency).

sections.p: Investigations are guided by the suspected cause and affected organ. They aim to assess the extent of atrophy and identify underlying pathologies.

t.a: Blood tests (e.g., hormone levels, nutritional markers)
t.b: To identify hormonal deficiencies or nutritional causes.
To measure organ size and detect structural changes.
Microscopic examination of tissue to confirm cellular changes.

sections.p: Severe atrophy can lead to irreversible loss of function. Complications include increased susceptibility to injury, infection, and failure of the affected organ system.
b: Organ failure (e.g., heart failure with cardiac atrophy).
Increased risk of fractures (e.g., osteoporosis).
Severe weakness and immobility.

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause. If the cause is irreversible or progressive, management aims to slow progression and manage symptoms.
b: Treat underlying cause (e.g., hormone replacement, nutritional support).
Physical therapy and exercise to stimulate muscle or tissue.
Supportive care to manage functional deficits.

sections.p: Follow-up depends on the cause and severity. Prevention involves addressing risk factors like malnutrition, immobility, and hormonal imbalances.
b: Regular monitoring of organ function.
Maintaining adequate nutrition and physical activity.
Addressing hormonal deficiencies promptly.

sections.p: Atrophy can be confused with hypoplasia (underdevelopment) or necrosis (cell death). Functional decline may also mimic other diseases.
b: Hypoplasia: organ is small from development, not shrinkage.
Necrosis: involves cell death, not just shrinkage.
Cachexia: generalised wasting, often due to chronic illness.

sections.p: Imaging may show reduced organ size that is normal for age or due to previous injury rather than active atrophy. Biopsies might miss atrophic areas if sampling is inadequate.
b: Age-related changes can mimic pathological atrophy.
Previous insults may cause permanent size reduction.
Intermittent causes may lead to normal findings between episodes.

faq.a: Mild atrophy, especially if caused by disuse or reversible factors, can sometimes be reversed with appropriate treatment and stimulation.

faq.q: Is atrophy a sign of aging?
faq.a: Some degree of atrophy is a normal part of aging (senile atrophy), but significant atrophy can be caused by various diseases.

faq.q: What is the difference between atrophy and hypertrophy?
faq.a: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size, while hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, usually in response to increased workload.
